steps.title: Short contact
steps.body: Most rosé is made from black grapes with skin contact of a few hours, then the juice is run off and fermented cool like a white. Direct pressing gives the palest colour, with juice just touched by the skins during the press. Longer maceration gives deeper colour and more fruit.
steps.highlight: Hours of contact, then made like a white

steps.title: Colour as a choice
steps.body: Rosé colour depends on grape, contact time and temperature. Thin-skinned Grenache gives pale pink quickly; thick-skinned Syrah colours fast. Provence's pale rosés, many with less than 6 hours of contact, now set the market fashion, so producers plan colour as carefully as flavour.
steps.highlight: Grape and contact time set the colour

steps.prompt: The rosé method that draws juice off a red wine tank is called ____.
steps.explanation: Saignée means bleeding. Pigeage and remontage are cap management methods for reds; dosage belongs to sparkling wine.

steps.title: Blending red and white
steps.body: In the EU, mixing red and white wine to make still rosé is not allowed. Champagne is the exception: most rosé Champagne is made by adding a small amount of still red wine to the white base. Outside Europe, blending is allowed in many countries.
steps.highlight: Blending is banned for most EU still rosé

steps.prompt: Which wine can legally be made by blending red and white wine in the EU?
steps.explanation: Rosé Champagne is the exception. Still rosé in the EU must be made from skin contact or saignée.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Most rosé is made with a short skin contact, then fermented like a white
Grape and contact time set the colour
Blending red and white is banned for EU still rosé, except Champagne
